findings.title: Path-item level `servers` leaks into every subsequent path when building the gorillamux router
findings.impact: `servers` is declared once outside the loop over paths and reassigned in place whenever a PathItem declares its own servers, but is never restored. Every path processed after such a path item is registered under the overriding servers' base path and host instead of the document-level ones. Depending on the iteration order produced by Paths.InMatchingOrder(), routes silently become unreachable (FindRoute returns ErrPathNotFound, so the operation is effectively dropped from validation) or become reachable only under a base path the specification never associated with them. Because openapi3filter.Validator.Middleware answers 404 on a routing miss, the failure mode is a quietly disabled endpoint rather than an obvious error.

findings.title: Unbounded slice allocation from an attacker-chosen deepObject array index (remote memory-exhaustion DoS)
findings.impact: Any service that validates requests with openapi3filter and has at least one style=deepObject query parameter whose schema contains an array can be OOM-killed or wedged by one unauthenticated ~30-byte request. The bracket index in the query key is used as the array length, not as a position to fill: sliceMapToSlice() takes max = the largest strconv.Atoi(index) and then materialises max+1 elements, and buildResObj() immediately allocates a second slice of the same size. `?param[items][2000000000]=1` asks the process for ~2e9 interface values (~32 GB across the two slices); `?param[items][9223372036854775807]=1` turns the fill loop into an effectively non-terminating allocation loop. This all happens during decoding, before any schema keyword is evaluated, so maxItems in the spec cannot prevent it. ValidateRequest does run ValidateSecurityRequirements before parameter decoding, so an endpoint with an enforced security requirement needs valid credentials first; any unauthenticated endpoint, any document without `security`, and any deployment using NoopAuthenticationFunc is exposed with no credentials at all.

findings.title: Encoding.Validate swallows its errors and returns nil, skipping the rest of the encoding checks
findings.impact: Inside the headers loop, both failure branches `return nil` instead of returning the error. An invalid encoding header name or an invalid header object is therefore reported as valid, and — because the function returns rather than continues — the serialization-method check and validateExtensions below never run for that Encoding at all. doc.Validate() consequently accepts documents it is supposed to reject, and any consumer relying on Validate() as its gate for spec well-formedness (including routers/legacy.NewRouter, which calls doc.Validate and treats success as a precondition) is operating on an unvalidated encoding.

findings.title: Compiled-pattern cache is keyed only by pattern text, so a custom Options.RegexCompiler is silently bypassed
findings.impact:
compiledPatterns is a process-wide sync.Map keyed on the pattern string alone, and compilePattern stores into it regardless of which compiler produced the matcher. Document validation compiles every `pattern` in the spec with the document-level compiler (usually the default Go regexp) and populates the cache; afterwards, request validation loads the cached matcher and never consults settings.regexCompiler. The result is that Options.RegexCompiler / SetSchemaRegexCompiler — which operators set precisely to get ECMA-262 semantics or a backtracking-safe / length-limited engine — has no effect on any pattern that was already compiled, and two documents in the same process that share a pattern string but configure different engines silently share one matcher. A validation control that the operator believes is in force is not.
The same block also has a nil-matcher path: when compilePattern fails and MultiError is on, cp holds a typed-nil matcher and cp.MatchString(value) is still called, panicking. That is reachable when the custom compiler rejects a pattern the default Go engine accepted.

findings.title: ValidationHandler defaults AuthenticationFunc to a no-op, turning declared security requirements into a fail-open
findings.impact: ValidationHandler.Load() substitutes NoopAuthenticationFunc when the embedder left AuthenticationFunc nil, so every security requirement in the document is considered satisfied and every request is admitted. This is the opposite of the library's own contract and of the other entry point: Options.AuthenticationFunc is documented as "A document with security schemes defined will not pass validation unless an AuthenticationFunc is defined", and validateSecurityRequirement returns ErrAuthenticationServiceMissing (fail-closed) when it is nil. A user who wires ValidationHandler expecting the documented fail-closed behaviour — or who removes their auth callback during a refactor — gets a silently unauthenticated endpoint instead of an error.

findings.title: ZipFileBodyDecoder appends the whole read buffer instead of the bytes actually read, corrupting the decoded content
findings.impact: The read loop appends all 256 bytes of the scratch buffer on every iteration regardless of how many bytes Read actually returned, so every short read (i.e. the tail of every entry, and any partial read in between) injects stale bytes left over from the previous iteration into the value. The string handed to schema validation is therefore not the content of the uploaded archive: validation decisions (pattern, maxLength, enum) are made against data the client never sent, in both directions — content can be smuggled past a pattern check and legitimate content can be rejected. The decoder is opt-in via RegisterBodyDecoder, and its own doc comment already warns it is zip-bomb-prone, which is the second reason not to expose it as written.

findings.title: OpenAPI 3.1+ documents silently lose readOnly/writeOnly enforcement, format assertions, custom format validators, the custom regex engine and default injection
findings.impact:
openapi3filter switches every 3.1/3.2 document onto the JSON Schema 2020-12 code path automatically and with no opt-out, and that path discards the schemaValidationSettings it is handed — useJSONSchema2020 receives `settings` and never uses it, calling validator.validate(value) instead. Everything expressed through settings therefore stops being enforced for 3.1+ specs, silently:
  - VisitAsRequest/VisitAsResponse: `readOnly: true` properties are no longer rejected in request bodies and `writeOnly: true` properties are no longer rejected in responses. Applications that use readOnly as their mass-assignment guard (id, role, isAdmin, balance, ownerId...) lose that guard the moment the spec is bumped from 3.0 to 3.1, with no error and no behaviour change anywhere else to signal it.
  - format: santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema v6 treats `format` as an annotation unless compiler.AssertFormat() is called, which newJSONSchemaValidator never does. `format: int32`, `date`, `date-time`, `byte`, `uuid` become no-ops, and every validator registered through DefineStringFormatValidator / WithStringFormatValidator(s) — including per-document validators plumbed in via Options.SchemaValidationOptions — is ignored.
  - Options.RegexCompiler, which deployments set precisely to swap Go's engine for a stricter or backtracking-safe one, is ignored.
  - DefaultsSet/default injection no longer runs, so documented defaults stop being applied to request bodies.
Because the compile-failure fallback is silent, behaviour also varies endpoint by endpoint inside the same document (a schema whose properties are $refs serialises as `{"$ref": "#/components/..."}` against a single anonymous compiler resource, typically fails to compile and quietly reverts to the built-in validator; a self-contained schema does not), which makes the weakening very hard to catch in testing.

openapi3/schema_jsonschema_validator.go:204-212:
	func (schema *Schema) useJSONSchema2020(settings *schemaValidationSettings, value any) error {
		validator, err := newJSONSchemaValidator(schema)
		if err != nil { return schema.visitJSON(settings, value) }   // silent fallback
		return validator.validate(value)                              // settings dropped on the floor
	}
openapi3/schema.go:1942-1949 VisitJSON: `if settings.useJSONSchema2020 { return schema.useJSONSchema2020(settings, value) }` — visitJSON, which is what actually implements readOnly/writeOnly (schema.go:2841-2857), format validators (2679-2707), pattern via settings.regexCompiler (2654-2660) and defaults (2843-2847), is bypassed entirely.
openapi3filter/validate_request.go:354 and openapi3filter/validate_response.go:76 enable it unconditionally: `if ...Spec.IsOpenAPI31OrLater() { opts = append(opts, openapi3.EnableJSO

findings.title: Nil-pointer dereference validating a response header declared with `content` instead of `schema`
findings.impact: validateResponseHeader assumes every documented response header has a `schema`, but OAS and this library's own openapi3.Header.Validate accept a header described with `content` and no `schema`. For such a header decodeValue() dereferences schema.Value on a nil *SchemaRef and the process panics. Any service using ValidateResponse or openapi3filter.Validator.Middleware with such a spec crashes on the first response that carries that header, i.e. a remote denial of service reachable by whatever request produces it.
findings.evidence:
openapi3filter/validate_response.go:181 `decodeValue(dec, headerName, sm, headerRef.Value.Schema, headerRef.Value.Required)` and :190 `headerRef.Value.Schema.Value.VisitJSON(decodedValue, opts...)` — neither checks headerRef.Value.Schema for nil.
openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:263-265 decodeValue() opens with `if len(schema.Value.AllOf) > 0 {`, an unguarded dereference of its *SchemaRef argument.
openapi3/header.go:73 permits the content-only form: `if (header.Schema == nil) == (len(header.Content) == 0) { return ...HeaderFieldValidationError }` — exactly one of schema/content must be set, so a content-only header passes document validation.

findings.title: Legacy router can return a nil route with a nil error, and dereferences a nil node on the same path
findings.impact: Router.FindRoute has a fall-through in which `route` is still nil: when pathpattern matching fails but doc.Paths holds the raw request path as a literal key and that PathItem defines the method, neither error return fires. Execution then reaches `paramKeys := node.VariableNames` with node == nil and panics the request goroutine. If node is non-nil but its Value is not a *routers.Route — which is exactly what AddRoute stores, it stores the *Router — the function instead returns (nil, pathParams, nil), and every caller (openapi3filter.ValidateRequest, ValidationHandler.validateRequest, Validator.Middleware) immediately dereferences route.Operation. Both outcomes are a remote crash, and the trigger is client-controlled: the pathpattern tree cannot match the literal text of template shapes it does not support (this package's own doc comment calls out `/books/{id}.json`), while doc.Paths.Value() matches that exact string, so a request for the literal templated URL walks straight into the gap.

findings.title: Default validation error text embeds the full schema and the submitted value, and the shipped error encoder writes it to the client
findings.impact: SchemaError.Error() appends a JSON dump of the whole failing *Schema and of the client's value unless the package-level SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled is flipped, and it defaults to false. ValidationHandler pairs this with DefaultErrorEncoder, which writes err.Error() straight into the HTTP response body. A client that sends a deliberately malformed field therefore gets back the internal schema for that endpoint — property names, enums, patterns, min/max, descriptions, and any internal field the public documentation omits — for the price of one bad request, plus an echo of its own input (a reflected-content channel if the response is ever rendered as HTML). It is also a footgun for the response side: ValidateResponse errors carry the server's own response value.
findings.evidence:
openapi3/schema.go:3118-3131:
	if !SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled {
		buf.WriteString("\nSchema:\n  "); encoder.Encode(err.Schema)
		buf.WriteString("\nValue:\n  "); encoder.Encode(err.Value)
	}
openapi3/schema.go:33-34 `SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled = false`.
openapi3filter/errors.go:23-38 RequestError.Error() concatenates the wrapped error's text verbatim.
openapi3filter/validation_kit.go:64-85 DefaultErrorEncoder writes `[]byte(err.Error())` to the ResponseWriter, and openapi3filter/validation_handler.go:50-52 installs it as the default for ValidationHandler.
(The same file's encoder.Encode calls are wrapped in `panic(err)` on marshal failure, at schema.go:3125 and 3129 — a second reason not to run this path while serving.)

advisories_to_match.summary: kin-openapi has uncontrolled resource consumption in openapi3filter deepObject query parameter decoding
advisories_to_match.description:
### Summary

An uncontrolled resource consumption vulnerability in `openapi3filter` lets any unauthenticated client force multi-gigabyte heap allocation with a single, tiny HTTP request. When a spec declares a `deepObject`-style query parameter whose schema contains an array (a normal, documented pattern), the decoder reconstructs the array by reading the **largest attacker-supplied index** and allocating one slot for every position from `0` up to that index — *before* schema validation (including `maxItems`) ever runs. A request as small as 24 bytes (`?param[items][50000000]=x`) drives heap allocation to **~6.1 GiB**, reliably triggering an OOM kill / restart loop on memory-constrained services.

### Details

The OpenAPI `style: deepObject` serialization lets clients express arrays in the query string using bracket notation, e.g. `param[items][0]=a&param[items][1]=b`. The decoder first collects these into an intermediate `map[string]any` keyed by the string of the index, then converts that sparse map into a real `[]any` in [`sliceMapToSlice`](https://github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/blob/master/openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go#L936):

```go
// req_resp_decoder.go (vulnerable versio
